live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a long-running espionage actor that goes after South Korean targets and policy circles
next.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is Secureworks' name for the group also called Kimsuky and APT43. Vendors and South Korean agencies tie it to phishing, fake installers and Android spyware, and most of them link it to North Korea.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for a threat actor that other vendors track as Kimsuky, APT43, Velvet Chollima, Emerald Sleet, THALLIUM, TA427 and many other names.
Microsoft, as relayed by BleepingComputer, describes Kimsuky as a North Korean state actor, also known as Emerald Sleet or Velvet Chollima.

A Sekoia and Kudelski Security overview says some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster made up of several branches, such as TA406 and TA408. It adds that vendors split and name clusters differently.

Genians says some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group. It says they overlap in targets and infrastructure. The MSMT report, as Genians cites it, assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes a command server it examined to Kimsuky (DPRK) with high confidence.
Microsoft says that since January 2025 Kimsuky has run limited attacks on people in international affairs groups, NGOs, government agencies and media companies.
Genians assesses with moderate confidence that Kimsuky ran a campaign against South Korean policy and security professionals. It notes a third party imitating the same techniques cannot be ruled out.
South Korea's National Police Agency said Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023.
AhnLab reported signs of Kimsuky's AppleSeed backdoor being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit in July 2022.
Breakglass Intelligence reports phishing lures aimed at South Korean users of the Naver web portal.

In the 2022 KAERI nuclear research breach, South Korean officials said the hackers were believed to operate from North Korea. One of the 13 IP addresses that abused a VPN flaw was linked to Kimsuky infrastructure.

Microsoft says Kimsuky adopted ClickFix-style tactics. A fake South Korean official contacts the target, sends a spear-phishing PDF, and tells the target to run attacker code in PowerShell. The code installs a browser-based remote desktop tool.

AhnLab describes spear-phishing with shortcut files disguised as documents. The chain delivers the PebbleDash backdoor and AsyncRAT, and it patches a Windows system file to bypass remote desktop authentication. AhnLab says Kimsuky has used PebbleDash since 2021.
South Korea's NCSC says Kimsuky compromised a construction trade website in January 2024 and used it to distribute trojanized security installers signed with a valid certificate.

ESRC reported in 2021 that Thallium altered the installer of a private stock investment messaging app. It also sent tainted installers and macro-laden Office documents, and it used a scheduled task for persistence.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new DOCSWAP Android malware to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean comments. ENKI says it could not confirm how victims were first reached. The RAT logs keystrokes and steals data.
S2W separately suspects a possible Kimsuky connection to DocSwap, a North Korea-linked Android spyware it tracks as puNK-004.
ESRC linked a February 2022 malicious Word document posing as a digital wallet service's customer guide to the Smoke Screen campaign and to Thallium, also known as Kimsuky.
The National Police Agency named Kimsuky in one of three cases of North Korean groups breaching South Korean defense firms and their subcontractors to steal technology data.

Breakglass Intelligence mapped about 79 domains across five IPs. It describes a three-stage chain that starts from a help file disguised as API documentation and ends in a keylogger with timed exfiltration.

Genians says the NodeLinkRAT campaign began with reply-based spearphishing from someone posing as a National Assembly member's aide. Later stages were swapped on a public note service, and XenoRAT was among the tools used.
Treat unexpected documents, shortcut files, installers and requests to run code as suspect, even when they come from a known contact or a familiar-looking site.
Keep VPN, email server and other exposed software patched, and use separate passwords for work and personal accounts.
